client: I've been really struggling since my grandmother passed away last month. At work, I keep zoning out during meetings and missing deadlines because I just can't focus. Then I feel guilty about not performing well, which makes the sadness even worse. To be honest, I'm not sure talking about it will help - the pain just feels too deep.
therapist: I hear how deeply this loss has affected you, and it makes complete sense that you're struggling to focus at work while carrying this heavy grief. The guilt you're feeling about work performance seems to be adding another layer of pain to an already difficult time—would you be willing to explore how these thoughts about work might be interacting with your grief?

client: I guess I haven't really thought about how the work stuff connects to the grief. It's just that when I try to focus at work, all I can think about is how I should have visited grandma more often. The guilt about work makes me feel like I'm failing at everything now - both as a granddaughter and as an employee.
therapist: It sounds like you're carrying two very heavy burdens—grief about your grandmother and self-criticism about not visiting more, which then spills over into feelings of failure at work. When those thoughts about "should have visited more" come up, have you noticed whether they feel like facts or if there might be other perspectives to consider?

client: They definitely feel like facts to me - I mean, I objectively could have visited more often. But I don't know... I was working so much even back then. It's not like I was just being lazy. Still, that doesn't make me feel any better about it now.
therapist: It sounds like you're caught between acknowledging the practical realities of your situation and still feeling deeply regretful about not visiting more. When you think about your intentions during that time—that you were working hard, not being lazy—does that perspective help soften some of the harshness you're directing toward yourself?

client: I guess it does help a little to remember that I wasn't just avoiding her - I was working hard. But it's still hard to shake the feeling that I should have made more time. Like maybe if I had prioritized better, I could have seen her more often. It's this constant back-and-forth in my head that's exhausting.
therapist: It sounds like you're caught in a cycle of "what ifs" that's leaving you emotionally drained. Would it be helpful to explore together how we might gently challenge those "should have" thoughts, while still honoring your feelings of loss and regret?

client: I guess it might help to challenge those thoughts, but part of me feels like I deserve to feel this guilt. Like if I stop beating myself up, it means I didn't care enough about her. It's complicated because I know logically that punishing myself won't bring her back, but emotionally it feels necessary.
therapist: I hear how deeply conflicted you feel—part of you recognizes logically that self-punishment isn't helping, while another part believes this guilt is a way to show your love and care for her. It sounds like you're grappling with a very human dilemma: How do we honor our loved ones without letting guilt consume us? What do you think your grandmother might say about the way you're treating yourself right now?

client: That question actually makes me tear up... Grandma was always so kind to me, even when I didn't visit as often as I wanted to. She'd probably tell me to stop being so hard on myself. But that's the thing - knowing she'd say that makes me feel even more guilty for not appreciating her kindness while she was here.
therapist: It sounds like remembering your grandmother's kindness brings up both warmth and pain—that beautiful yet bittersweet feeling of loving someone so deeply. The fact that you can recognize what she would say shows how well you knew her heart, and perhaps that very connection could be a starting point for healing rather than guilt. Would you be willing to explore how you might honor her kindness by extending some of that same compassion toward yourself?

client: That's a really beautiful way to think about it, but it feels so hard to imagine being kind to myself right now. It's like I'm caught between wanting to honor her kindness and feeling like I don't deserve it because I wasn't there for her enough. The idea of extending compassion to myself feels foreign, almost like I'd be letting her down somehow.
therapist: It sounds like you're standing at a crossroads between the loving memories of your grandmother and these painful feelings of unworthiness—and that in-between space can feel so uncomfortable. When you say extending compassion feels like letting her down, I wonder what it might look like to view self-compassion not as something you deserve, but as something she would want for the granddaughter she clearly loved so much?

client: That perspective makes me cry, but in a different way. It's hard to imagine grandma would want me suffering like this - she always hated seeing me upset. But old habits die hard, you know? The guilt has become such a familiar feeling that the idea of letting it go almost feels scary, like I'd be losing some connection to her.
therapist: It sounds like you're holding onto this guilt almost as a way to stay connected to your grandmother, even though you know in your heart she wouldn't want you to suffer. That tension between wanting to honor her memory and wanting to heal from the pain is so understandable. What do you think it might look like to find a new way to feel connected to her that doesn't involve self-punishment?

client: I never thought about finding other ways to stay connected to her... Maybe I could start doing things she loved, like baking her favorite recipes. But part of me worries that would just remind me of all the times I didn't bake with her when I had the chance. It feels safer to stay stuck in the guilt than risk feeling her absence even more.
therapist: I hear how torn you feel between wanting to honor her memory through baking and fearing it might intensify the pain of her absence—that's such a natural part of grieving. But I also notice something hopeful in your words: you're beginning to imagine new possibilities for connection, even as you wrestle with these fears. What would it feel like to try just one small baking experiment, while being gentle with yourself about whatever emotions might come up?

client: I guess I could try baking her famous apple pie this weekend... but I'm scared I'll just end up crying the whole time and feeling worse. What if it's too painful and I can't finish it? Then I'll feel like I failed at honoring her memory too.
therapist: It's completely understandable to feel nervous about how emotional this might be—grief has a way of surprising us in these moments. But what if we reframe this: rather than seeing tears as failure, could we view them as part of the honoring, as evidence of how deeply you loved her? How might it feel to give yourself full permission to experience whatever comes up during this baking experiment?
